title: Do education programmes for children and young people with disabilities in low- and middle-income countries work?

blocks.html: The question is: “In low- and middle-income countries, do programmes meant to improve education for children and young people with disabilities work, and which kinds work best?”

sentences: A 2025 Campbell systematic review concludes that a range of individual-level interventions work to improve educational outcomes among people with disabilities in low- and middle-income countries, but that there is little research on systemic or school-level change [1].
The review's authors describe the evidence as providing "emerging support" for these interventions rather than settled proof [1].

The clearest effects reported are for interventions that build learners' skills, such as literacy, cognitive skills, handwriting and numeracy, but these large effects are based on a low number of studies [1].
Interventions that change schools, systems or environments have been studied much less, so the passages cannot say whether they work better or worse [1, 2, 3].
People with disabilities often fall behind their peers in enrolment, retention and completion of education, and the gap in educational attainment is largest in low- and middle-income countries [1].
Before the 2025 review, its authors noted that evidence on which interventions are actually effective had not been established [1].
Of the 18 studies included in the review's analysis of effects on 'Skills for learning', 12 interventions had a significant effect [1].
By outcome, effects on literacy, cognitive skills, handwriting and numeracy were significant, and the review says all these effects are large but based on a low number of studies [1].
Studies concerned with 'Conditions for inclusion of people with disabilities in education' showed a moderately significant effect [1].
One study concerned with teacher knowledge showed a significant effect size [1].

An evidence and gap map of teacher professional development for disability inclusion in Asia-Pacific low- and middle-income countries found 50 studies, with only 16 of 41 countries reporting evidence [2].
In that map, a significant number of interventions focused on changing teacher attitudes and understanding of disability [2].
Only three studies in the map addressed student mental health [2].
No studies in the map reported on how teachers could support positive student behaviour [2].
Some included studies were qualitative [2].
In one such study from Vietnam, teachers reported that training seminars and workshops improved the general quality of teaching in their schools [2].
Most interventions in the 2025 review tried to improve children's skills and did not focus on system-level or school-level changes [1].

A broader evidence and gap map on disability in low- and middle-income countries likewise found that studies mostly try to change characteristics of the person with a disability rather than address structures such as schools' readiness to include them [3].
That map also found that fewer studies focus on improving infrastructure or institutions [3].
Over half of the impact evaluations in that map came from upper-middle income countries, with only 9 from low-income countries [3].
The same map reports a significant gap in study quality, especially for impact evaluations [3].
In the 2025 review, the interventions and outcome measures were all different, making direct comparison difficult [1].
None of the studies in the 2025 review were in humanitarian settings, and few disaggregated their findings by gender [1].

blocks.text: Which kinds work best for which disabilities

sentences: The 2025 review set out to ask which interventions appear most effective for different types of disability [1].
None of the passages provided here reports its answer to that question.

It holds up that a range of individual-level, skills-focused interventions improve educational outcomes for learners with disabilities in low- and middle-income countries, though the reviewers call this support "emerging" [1].
Skills-building interventions show the most consistent evidence, but the large effects on literacy, numeracy and related skills rest on a low number of studies [1].
Whether school-level or systemic approaches work best cannot be judged from this evidence, because such approaches have been little studied [1, 3].
The 2025 review's authors say more systemic approaches are needed to improve access to, and successful engagement in, education [1].
The authors call for studies with larger samples, more rigorous designs and standardised measures [1].
